D. Stand directly in line with the table saw blade without eye protection so you can hold the board down if it starts to kick back.

pamphlet_excerpts: Bucking Felled Tree Trunks: Then workers called buckers lop off the limbs and slice the trunks into shorter lengths (logs) that are easier to handle (p. 14).
Transporting Logs to Sawmills: The logs are trucked, floated, or carried on railroads to asawmill (p. 14).
Debarking and Sawing Boards: At the mill, logs are debarked (their bark is removed), and saws cut them into boards (lumber) (p. 14).
Gang Sawing Small Logs: Small logs are often cut into boards in a single pass through a set of saws (a gang saw) that makes many cuts at once (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Debark Logs Before Sawing: At the mill, logs are debarked (their bark is removed), and saws cut them into boards (lumber) (p. 14).
Step 2 - Mill Small Logs Together: Small logs are often cut into boards in a single pass through a set of saws (a gang saw) that makes many cuts at once (p. 14).
Step 3 - Slice Large Logs Repeatedly: Large logs may make several passes through one saw (a head saw) that slices off a board at a time until the whole log is cut into lumber (p. 14).
Step 4 - Edge and Trim Boards: The new lumber, called green lumber, is edged and trimmed to straighten the sides and cut into boards of standard lengths (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: Dangers of Dull Blades: You are more likely to mar your work and injure yourself with a dull blade than a sharp one because dull blades require extra force and can slip (p. 34).
Preventing Edge Nicks: Rough handling will nick and dull the cutting edges (p. 34).
Ground and Sharpening Bevels: Most wood-cutting tools have two wedge shapes on their cutting edge, the main or ground bevel, and the sharpening bevel (p. 34).
Honing the Secondary Bevel: When you are sharpening an edge, you should be working off the sharpening bevel only, not the larger ground bevel (p. 34).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Dual Edge Bevels: Most wood-cutting tools have two wedge shapes on their cutting edge, the main or ground bevel, and the sharpening bevel (p. 34).
Step 2 - Hone the Sharpening Bevel: When you are sharpening an edge, you should be working off the sharpening bevel only, not the larger ground bevel (p. 34).
Step 3 - Progress Through Stone Grits: When sharpening a blade, start with a roughs tone, followed by (in this order and as needed) a medium, fine, and smooth stone (p. 34).
Step 4 - Push Edge Forward Smoothly: Whet the edge by pushing it forward over the stone (p. 34).

pamphlet_excerpts: Mortise and Tenon Anatomy: The mortise is a hole in one piece of wood, and the tenon is the part of the second piece that is cut and shaped (p. 60).
Drilling Out the Mortise: Simply, this joint is "a square peg in a square hole." To start the mortise, drill the holes only as deep as you want the mortise (p. 60).
Chiseling Square Mortise Corners: Then use a sharp wood chisel to shave out any excess wood and square the corners (p. 60).
Marking Tenon Depth Dimensions: To make the tenon, mark its depth and width on the end of the tenon piece (p. 60).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Chisel Mortise Corners Square: Then use a sharp wood chisel to shave out any excess wood and square the corners (p. 60).
Step 2 - Lay Out Tenon Dimensions: To make the tenon, mark its depth and width on the end of the tenon piece (p. 60).
Step 3 - Saw Straight Tenon Cheeks: Use a back saw to cut the tenon, making a series of straight, square cuts to remove excess wood (p. 60).
Step 4 - Fit Tenon Into Mortise: Think of "tenant", someone who dwells inside a place, to help you remember that the tenon (the peg) goes inside the mortise (the hole) (p. 60).

pamphlet_excerpts: Defining Mortise and Tenon: The mortise is a hole in one piece of wood, and the tenon is the part of the second piece that is cut and shaped (p. 62).
Drilling Controlled Mortise Depths: Simply, this joint is "a square peg in a square hole." To start the mortise, drill the holes only as deep as you want the mortise (p. 62).
Squaring Recessed Joint Walls: Then use a sharp wood chisel to shave out any excess wood and square the corners (p. 62).
Measuring Tenon Shoulder Lines: To make the tenon, mark its depth and width on the end of the tenon piece (p. 62).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Pare Mortise Walls Square: Then use a sharp wood chisel to shave out any excess wood and square the corners (p. 62).
Step 2 - Mark Tenon Shoulder Lines: To make the tenon, mark its depth and width on the end of the tenon piece (p. 62).
Step 3 - Saw Straight Tenon Shoulders: Use a back saw to cut the tenon, making a series of straight, square cuts to remove excess wood (p. 62).
Step 4 - Assemble Peg Into Socket: Think of "tenant", someone who dwells inside a place, to help you remember that the tenon (the peg) goes inside the mortise (the hole) (p. 62).
